checked.summary:
Skeptic pass. I re-opened every URL with Firecrawl only. All four core PDFs were re-read in full: SCTE 293-5 (11 pp), SCTE 293-7 (12 pp), SCTE 180 2025 (168 pp) and ANSI/SCTE 279 2022 (41 pp). The two large PDFs were too big to return inline, so I read the saved Firecrawl output locally. I also re-checked the CableLabs and SCTE catalog pages, the SCTE Standards Updates page and the SCTE FAQ. No third-party mirrors were used.

Nearly every first-pass value reproduced exactly. That includes the SCTE 293-5 definitions and Figure 2/3 numbers, all SCTE 293-7 example levels, SCTE 180 Tables 12 and 13 row by row, and the SCTE 279 test-point, gain and control clauses.

Corrections made:
(a) SCTE 180's free-release announcement is under the November 2025 heading of SCTE Standards Updates. This settles the first pass's November/December uncertainty. The PDF release date remains 10/20/2025.
(b) The claim that the SCTE 293-5 catalog page title includes 'Log In' did not reproduce. The page title is 'What is…Unity Gain? — SCTE'.
(c) In SCTE 180 13.3.1.2, the last step says to confirm 'the output levels' at the amplifier output test point. It does not say forward levels.
(d) The SCTE 279 booster rule against adjustable upstream gain or slope is §10.5.1 (p.34), not §10.3.
(e) 'UGRP' is the first pass's shorthand. SCTE 180 never uses that abbreviation; it writes 'unity gain reference point'.
(f) The 'not-found' entry for the SCTE Measurement Recommended Practices is contradicted. The Fifth Edition is SCTE 183 2023, an SCTE Operational Practice of 376 pages, downloadable free from CableLabs. Its TOC lists tutorial 16.4 'Return Plant Setup and Operational Practices' (p.296), Figure 16-13 'Typical Amplifier Station Showing Reference Point Choices', Table 16-6 'Level References and their Relationship' and §6.3 'Frequency Response - Return'. I could not read that content: four full-length Firecrawl PDF scrapes timed out. Only the first 14 pages were read.
(g) SCTE 297 is 2025r1, an SCTE Operational Practice from the Network Operations Subcommittee. Its PDF release history lists 'SCTE 297 2025, 5/19/2025'. The SCTE catalog summary says the method lets a technician determine unity gain and flatness from the node to the ends of line.
(h) SCTE 180 page numbers come from the document's own TOC and lists of figures and tables. That TOC is inconsistent elsewhere (§7 is listed at p.21, after §6.8 at p.22), and pages were not checked against printed footers.

What the sources establish for the feature:
- SCTE 293-5 defines unity gain as each amplifier's gain equalling the loss of the span upstream of it. The forward reference point is the amplifier output. The return reference point is each return amplifier's input, which footnote 7 places at the common point of the output diplex filter.
- SCTE 180 2025 is the operational basis for the worksheet and the done check:
  - Rough balance is setting near-correct levels with an SLM. Sweep, or system alignment, is precise amplitude-versus-frequency alignment.
  - Verification testing comes after both.
  - The return path holds a constant input at the unity gain reference point.
  - The sweep reference is stored with the source injected at the node.
  - Source level = desired level at the reference point + (test point loss + loss from test point to gain block − loss from reference point to gain block).
  - Pad and EQ are adjusted until the headend response matches the reference.
  - All balancing and sweep results should be kept in a per-amplifier history file. A sample amplifier data sheet is given in Figure 131.
  - SCTE 180 gives no numeric headend receive target.
- SCTE 293-7 is about DOCSIS long-loop ALC (the CMTS receive set point, 0 dBmV by default and configurable). It is not plant alignment.
- ANSI/SCTE 279 is a 1.8 GHz FDD amplifier product specification that never mentions unity gain. It does define -20 dB test points (upstream accuracy ±1 dB), an upstream injection point on the diplex common path, and the split options in Table 1 (sub-split 42/54, mid-split 85/108, high-split 204/258 MHz, and others). It requires electronic upstream pad and EQ with no plug-ins, and Table 5 lists reportable upstream attenuation and EQ settings.

items.appliesTo: Unity gain definition (forward and return)
items.values: Paraphrase of 4.2: unity gain is a design and operating philosophy in which each amplifier's gain in dB equals the total loss in dB of the coax and passives immediately upstream of that amplifier, so the net gain from amplifier to amplifier is 0 dB. 'Unity' means a gain of 1, i.e. 0 dB. Gain GdB = Pout(dBmV) - Pin(dBmV); loss LdB = Pin(dBmV) - Pout(dBmV). Attenuator (pad): a passive part that lowers RF power without appreciable distortion. Equalizer (in this document's context): a passive part with roughly the opposite loss-versus-frequency of a given length of coax.
items.locator: Section 4.2 Definitions (TOC p.6; table continues onto p.7)

items.appliesTo: Forward (downstream) amplifiers
items.values: 5.1: with forward unity gain, the input level to a span equals the output level of the amplifier right after that span (exceptions exist, e.g. a bridger feeding a derated line extender). Cascade example: 10 identical amps with 22 dB gain and 23 dB span loss. First output +32 dBmV, second input +9 / output +31 dBmV, third input +8 / output +30 dBmV, tenth input +1 / output +23 dBmV. 5.1.1 / Figure 2: identical 22 dB amps, output +32 dBmV. Span AB 22 dB @ 750 MHz gives +10 dBmV input (0 dB input atten.). Span BC is 2 dB coupler + 14 dB cable @ 750 MHz = 16 dB, so a 6 dB input attenuator gives +16 dBmV input. Span BD totals 19 dB (Figure 2 shows 8 dB and 11 dB @ 750 MHz), so a 3 dB input attenuator gives +13 dBmV input. All outputs are +32 dBmV. The forward unity gain reference point is the downstream amplifier output. In a cascade of identical amps, one objective is identical levels at the reference points.
items.locator: Section 5.1 and Figure 1 (p.8); Section 5.1.1 and Figure 2 (p.9), reference-point statement (p.10); footnote 6 (p.9)

items.appliesTo: Return (upstream/reverse) amplifiers
items.values: 5.1.2: return unity gain in the cascade is essential. A return amp's gain must numerically equal the loss of the cable and passives in the span immediately upstream of it. The return reference point is at the same physical place as the forward one, but in signal-flow terms it is each amplifier's input. Footnote 7: the upstream amplifier input means the common point of the (downstream) output diplex filter, often the same physical location as the housing's downstream output port. Figure 3 (losses at 30 MHz, identical 15 dB return amps, each reference-point input +20 dBmV): span AB 4 dB needs an 11 dB output attenuator at amp B (output +24 dBmV); span BC 5 dB needs 10 dB at amp C (output +25 dBmV); span BD (8 dB passive + 2 dB cable) needs 5 dB at amp D (output +30 dBmV). The objective is identical levels at the reference points (the reverse amp inputs). Pads and EQs go at return amp outputs because amp B is fed by both spans BC and BD, so one input pad at B cannot correct both.

items.appliesTo: What long loop ALC is
items.values: 4.2: ALC is a closed-loop process that keeps configured RF levels at a circuit, device or network input or output when levels change from external factors such as attenuation. Net upstream attenuation is all gains and losses between a cable modem and the CMTS/CCAP/remote PHY input; example: modem +45 dBmV, CMTS input 0 dBmV, so 45 dB. The upstream definition gives sub-split 5-42 MHz, mid-split 5-85 MHz, high-split 5-204 MHz, and up to 684 MHz in some applications. Section 5: in DOCSIS station maintenance (defined in MULPI), the CMTS checks the received level and timing. If the level does not match the target set point (default 0 dBmV in most CMTSs, user configurable), it sends an RNG-RSP telling the modem to change its transmit power. Footnote 2: the target is the receive level set point (RLSP), formerly 'commanded nominal receive power' in DOCSIS 3.0 and earlier. Footnote 3: coax attenuation in dB changes about 1% for every 10 °F. Boxed note: added attenuation lowers all RF levels by that amount; only the modem's transmit power changes to make it up.

items.appliesTo: Upstream level behavior when attenuation changes
items.values: 5.1.1 baseline: modem DS input +3 dBmV, modem US transmit +45 dBmV, tap input +43 dBmV, node +15 dBmV, CMTS 0 dBmV. 5.1.2: a four-way splitter adds 7 dB. Before ranging: tap +36, node +8, CMTS -7 dBmV, DS at modem -4 dBmV. After RNG-RSP the modem goes to +52 dBmV, and tap +43, node +15, CMTS 0 dBmV are restored (DS stays -4). 5.1.3: a 3 dB pad at the CMTS upstream input briefly gives -3 dBmV. Modems on that port then rise 3 dB (+45 to +48), so tap +46, node +18 (also the upstream optical receiver output), and pad input +3 dBmV. Benefit: upstream CNR improves by the pad value. Risks: laser clipping if the optical link is near compression, and modems already at maximum transmit cannot follow. 5.1.4: with a +54 dBmV modem maximum and 10 dB of extra drop loss, the modem rises only 9 dB, so tap +42, node +17, CMTS -1 dBmV, DS -7 dBmV. The fix is to repair the drop.

items.appliesTo: Return alignment versus long loop ALC
items.values: Stated: anything that changes net upstream attenuation between modems and the CMTS makes the CMTS change modem transmit power (Section 5). Padding at the headend or hub raises upstream levels in the coax plant and at the node, with a laser-clipping risk (5.1.3). Not stated: SCTE 293-7 does not cover return sweep, injection levels, amplifier pads/EQs or unity gain reference points. Inference (labeled): ALC corrects only the end-to-end total, so return amplifier unity gain still decides where modem transmit and node input levels settle. SCTE 180 13.7.1 supports this indirectly: a poorly chosen reference point causes different modem levels in homes depending on amp type.

items.appliesTo: Done check: balanced versus swept
items.values: 5.2 definitions: Rough Balance is coarse adjustment of amplifiers and other devices, often during initial setup of new, upgraded or rebuilt plant. Sweep is the general term for precise alignment or maintenance of a cable network or its parts using a sweep generator or sweep transmitter and a companion receiver. 13.2.2.1: rough balancing means setting proper RF levels with a signal level meter (SLM). It gets near-correct levels at the actives so tap levels are adequate for initial installation, and should be done before adding customers. 13.3: system alignment is amplitude-versus-frequency (sweep) testing, used at initial turn-on and in ongoing maintenance. 13.3.1: it assumes the headend and optical link are set up, and it starts at the node and works toward end of line. 13.4: verification testing (CCN, MER, CSO, CTB, hum) should be done after rough balance and sweep testing are completed.

items.appliesTo: Return path balancing concept and methods
items.values: 13.2.2.2: the return has many customer inputs feeding one headend/node return input. One return amp causing distortion can degrade the whole return node, so the return should be balanced before the headend/node return input is connected to the existing system. Initial return balancing means placing the proper pad and EQ in the return amps to keep headend/node noise and ingress low. 13.2.2.2.2: forward amps are set for constant output level; return amps are set for constant input level. The return monitoring point (the next amp's input) is some distance from the amp under test. Three methods: video monitor with a multi-carrier generator; SLM with an upstream carrier generator; return sweep system. When the correct level is injected at the return amp's unity gain reference point, the correct input to the headend equipment results, so the headend reading is referenced to the source injected at the amplifier.

items.appliesTo: Return sweep equipment setup, injection and receive points
items.values: 13.2.2.3.3.1 legacy method (Figure 128): a headend spectrum analyzer is viewed by a camera carried on an unused forward channel (needs an unused 6 MHz downstream channel), with a return signal source injecting at the amp. Dedicated return sweep (Figure 129): a headend monitor measures the field unit's return signals and sends the frequency response back on a forward telemetry carrier. The field unit controls the headend monitor and has a built-in source to inject known signals at the field test point. Modes: return sweep and ingress monitor. Setup: program telemetry carriers and a sweep table that avoids active return signals. Store a trace of the headend reading with the signal injected at the node as the reference, and compare later injection points against it. The reference level relates to the constant input level required at each return amp's unity gain reference point. Forward RF output goes to the field unit RF input; field unit source output goes to the return injection point. 13.2.2.3.3.2: check ingress before return monitor mode. Check the return attenuator and EQ against the design drawing. Connect the proper-level source at the return injection point (level per 13.7.2) and check headend levels, which should be close to correct. Use gain/slope controls (if present) for fine adjustment. Small pad/EQ changes are fine; if the required values differ significantly from design, find and fix the problem before continuing.

items.appliesTo: Return amplifier sweep alignment step
items.values: 13.3.1.2: the return measurement device is usually at the headend, with display data sent on a downstream telemetry carrier. Testing needs a known, calibrated signal source at the amp under test. Set the return sweep transmitter output equal to the level required at the unity gain reference point plus the loss between the insertion point and the reference point. A sweep source level matrix per amplifier type can simplify this (see 13.7.2). Connect the source at the return insertion point and compare the headend sweep response with the reference. Adjust attenuator and EQ values until the response matches the reference. Different insertion point types may need different source levels. Then connect the receiver to the amplifier output test point and confirm the output levels, close and secure the housing, and go to the next station.

items.appliesTo: Where the return unity gain reference point is
items.values: 13.7.1: the forward path needs constant amplifier output (forward unity gain, output to output). The return path needs constant input to every amplifier (return unity gain, amp to amp). That input is at the unity gain reference point, which may be the return gain block (hybrid), the common port of the diplex filter, or the amplifier station input port. It is set during design. Historically the gain block input was used (long trunk cascades, analog return video), but station-port-to-gain-block loss differs by amp type: very little in a line extender, up to 8 dB additional combining loss in a four-port amplifier. That caused different home modem levels by amp type, which modern networks cannot tolerate. Unity gain at the amp port is now preferred, and most modern designs use the diplex filter common port as the more exact reference point. The reference point may not be reachable from a test point, so the source output should exceed the desired reference-point input by a factor calculated per amp or node type. Figure 133 (Generic Amplifier Diagram) marks a 'Return Hybrid Unity Gain Reference Point' and a 'Diplex Filter Unity Gain Reference Point'.

After choosing the injection level, make sure the headend receiver is set correctly for the received level. A matrix can be made for any return insertion point (nodes, amps, tap ports), and for a tap location the tap value may replace test point loss.

items.appliesTo: Return balancing preconditions
items.values: 13.7.3: ingress (shortwave, CB/ham, power-line and appliance noise) enters where shielding is compromised (loose connectors, cracked cable, loose or warped lids, loose tap plates), is amplified, and builds up at the headend. Poor return alignment affects plant noise and ingress. Powering return amps with 0 dB return attenuator/EQ can make enough noise in a few amps to disable the whole return, which is why return levels are set before the path is combined with the active system. If ingress disrupts sweep telemetry, isolate it by disconnecting return inputs or temporarily removing return attenuators; some amps have plug-in diplex filters and splitters. Some sweep systems broadcast ingress measurements to the field unit when a threshold is exceeded. 13.2.1.1.1: check return amp operation as soon as possible after energizing; excessive ingress will disable the existing system's return, and in that case the return amp should be disabled until it is fixed.

items.appliesTo: Forward side of the station view (new in this pass)
items.values: 13.2.2.2.1: at each station check AC voltage, DC voltage and RF input level against the design map before setting outputs. If inputs deviate from design, find and fix the problem before balancing continues. Apply equalizers first for slope; pads lower all frequencies equally. 13.2.2.3.2: SLM at the input test point to compare upper and lower reference (balance) carriers with design. Turn off AGC (if applicable), measure at the output test point, and compare pad and EQ with design. Set the upper carrier with the pad (coarse) and gain control (fine) for ambient temperature per the manufacturer; set the lower carrier with the EQ (coarse) and slope control (fine). Recheck, then turn AGC on and set the AGC gain control (pad per manufacturer). 13.3.1.1 (sweep): compare input levels with design for current ambient temperature. Check the sweep response; major suck-outs or variations should be corrected before proceeding, because signature correction only covers up problems. Pad/EQ must match the design maps, or the mismatch goes to the system engineer before proceeding. Manual-gain amps: set output to design. AGC/ALC amps: follow the manufacturer. Adjust signature controls for a flat response and check each output test point on multi-output amps.

items.appliesTo: Amplifier RF test points (high-gain and booster)
items.values: 7.2.7 (high gain, downstream): each downstream output port shall have a directional test point; the downstream input port shall have one (may be directional). All downstream test points shall be -20 dB relative to the port. Output test points should be accurate to -20 dB +/- 0.5 dB and shall be accurate to -20 dB +/- 1.0 dB. Downstream output test points shall be on the diplex common path so they also serve for upstream injection with two-way test gear. 7.3.7 (high gain, upstream): each upstream input port shall have a directional input test point; the upstream output port shall have one (may be directional). Each upstream input port shall also have an upstream RF injection test point on the diplex common path, which doubles as the downstream output test point. All upstream test points shall be -20 dB relative to the reference point and accurate to -20 dB +/- 1 dB. Test point type, loss and accuracy at room temperature shall be published; measurements per SCTE 144. Booster: 10.2.7 downstream test points are -20 dB, accurate to +/- 1.5 dB; 10.3.7 upstream test points are -20 dB relative to the port, accurate to +/- 1.5 dB, plus an upstream injection test point on the diplex common path. 9.1.4: high-gain strand-mount amps use a male G-connector test port; high-gain cabinet-mount (compact) amps use a female F-connector.

items.values: 7.3.1: upstream passband should be 5 to 684 MHz and shall be at least 10 to 492 MHz. 7.3.2 (high gain): upstream operational gain is station gain at the highest rated frequency from upstream input to output with other ports terminated, including back-off for quasi-AGC and/or thermal level control where applicable. The amount is left to the manufacturer; at publication it was anticipated that gain at 684 MHz for high-gain amps 'may need to be in the 30-32 dB range'. The minimum room-temperature gain per split and mode shall be published, specified for the station (inclusive of input losses) with 0 dB input and 0 dB output attenuation, measured per SCTE 144. 10.3.2 (booster): anticipated 4 to 7 dB at 684 MHz. 7.3.3: upstream internal slope, if adjustable, in increments no greater than 0.5 dB. 7.3.4: upstream frequency response shall not exceed ±1.0 dB relative to internal slope. checked.summary:
This re-check is only partly done. Firecrawl credits ran out after 7 successful calls. All 7 were on the System Amplifier (SA) guide PDF on manuals.plus (a third-party mirror). Three more SA queries failed: identity and back cover, accessory tables, and Appendix A EQ charts. Credits reset at 2026-11-11T23:09Z. Because of that, I could not re-open the Line Extender (LE) PDF, the manualzz copy, the two Cisco data sheets, the Cisco OL/4009927 URLs or the Wayback URLs. Every item that rests only on those sources is downgraded to not-found, with values left empty. Its notes say that this means "not re-verified", not "absent from the source".

Reproduced in the SA mirror (title in the PDF metadata, 132 pages, copyright 2008, 2013-2014 Cisco):
- Table of contents: Balancing the Reverse Path p.72 (About p.72, Prepare p.73, Calculate p.74, Complete p.76). No Reverse RF Signal p.88; Low or Degraded Reverse p.89. Reverse EQ charts: 42/40 MHz p.98, 42/40 thermal p.99, 55 MHz p.99, 65 MHz p.100. Attenuator part numbers p.102; reverse EQ part numbers p.106; thermal p.107. There is no 85 MHz chart. The in-text cross-references match the TOC.
- Order of work: balance the reverse fiber link first, then each cascade from the amplifier nearest the node outward, from each split, and on every node port.
- Injection: signals of known level go in at the Main, Aux 1 or Aux 2 "Forward Output and Reverse Injection" test point, ahead of the reverse amplifier.
- Injection level = design reverse port input level + 20 dB total injection insertion loss. Example: 19 dBmV + 20 dB = 39 dBmV.
- Input pad: the design reverse input pads come after the injection point. Either swap in a temporary 0 dB pad, which keeps injection and receive levels constant from amp to amp and port to port, or expect a receive level x dB lower. Put the design pads back afterwards.
- Read point: the RF test point on the output of the node's reverse optical receiver in the headend or hub. Generator and sweep offsets shift the reference 1:1.
- Fix tilt with the reverse output EQ. Fix level with the reverse output pad: +1 dB of pad gives -1 dB of receive level.
- Done when the receive level and tilt match the reference.
- High Gain Dual minimum reverse input pads: Splitter 3.5/3.5, DC-8 8.0/2.0, DC-12 12.0/1.5.
- Test point adapter 562580 or F-81.

New finding: the forward procedures give a ±0.5 dB tolerance against design tilt and level. The reverse section gives no numeric tolerance at all. So the app's balanced and swept criteria (balanced vs swept) must come from company sources. The reverse section I read contains no 'unity' wording.

Corrections to the first pass:
- The Description list in the extracted SA text shows HGD, LGD, HGBT, HO HGBT and GaN HGBT. UBT appears elsewhere (TOC, AGC pad formula). HO HGD and GaN HGD were not seen.
- The extracted pad sentence reads 'the reverse input comes after the reverse injection point'. The word 'pad' is missing from the text layer.
- The first pass said the guide refers readers to the sweep maker's guide, that it says to check the fiber link first, and that it says to balance all amps off one node port in sequence. None of these could be reproduced.
- OL-31156-01 and February 2014 were not reproduced in this pass.

items.values: Balancing means aligning each reverse amplifier station's gain and tilt individually so the reverse cascades have optimum, repeatable transmission characteristics. The process is the same whatever test equipment is used. Order: (1) balance the reverse fiber link, i.e. node reverse optical transmitter to headend/hub reverse optical receiver; (2) balance the reverse amplifier cascades that combine at the node, starting with the amplifier closest to the node and working outward toward the first reverse amplifier in each upstream cascade. After each station reaches the proper receive level and tilt, close the housing and repeat at the next reverse amplifier in the downstream cascade. Work outward from the node and from each external split until the cascade is done. Repeat for the cascades off every remaining active node port.

items.values: Tilt is the level difference between the highest and lowest frequencies in the reverse passband, or between the highest and lowest frequency CW test signals. Most systems want minimal reverse tilt (flat levels) at the headend. To reduce tilt, change the amplifier reverse output equalizer. To match the desired reference level, change the amplifier reverse output pad: each 1 dB increase in pad gives a 1 dB decrease in receive level, and each 1 dB decrease gives a 1 dB increase. Once the proper receive level and tilt are reached, close the housing and move to the next reverse amplifier.

checked.summary:
I could not run the skeptic pass. Firecrawl rejected the first three re-check calls (ManualsLib viewer pages 60, 61 and 62) with "Insufficient credits", and its error told agents not to retry. The daily MCP allowance resets at 2026-11-11T23:09:02Z. The task allows only Firecrawl tools, so no URL, value, page, revision or date below was re-opened or reproduced. Every item still has its first-pass status and values, and each note now says it was not re-verified. Run this pass again after the credit reset, before the app relies on any item as checked twice.

What the first pass says the sources establish (not re-checked):
(1) AOI Quantum18 SA guide V02102025, read through the ManualsLib third-party mirror only.
- Upstream alignment comes after downstream setup of the whole cascade and starts at the last amplifier. It runs in Auto mode (ends with a Save or Revert prompt) or Manual mode.
- Manual mode uses an ONX-630 in DOCSIS Expert mode. Only Gain and Tilt are adjusted, one at a time, against marker levels. Changes are applied, then saved or reverted.
- ALSC is off by default and is turned ON on each amplifier after both directions are aligned.
- The test points are -20 dB and their routing is chosen in the app.
- The vendor claims auto-alignment gives unity gain without field measurements.
- The troubleshooting page gives a reverse gain check using input/output test points, pad values and EQ insertion loss, but it carries a draft marker.
- No injection level, reference level, gain/tilt range or step size appears in the text. The 750 MHz upstream example table is an image only.

(2) AOI QB18 HGD data sheet (PRELIMINARY; Internet Archive capture of 2024-11-07). Reverse figures, all for the 204 MHz split: minimum gain 27 dB, internal tilt 0 dB, recommended input 9 dBmV per 6.4 MHz, noise figure <9 dB, 10 dB dynamic range at NPR >= 55 dB.

(3) VIAVI return sweep.
- The field ONX injects telemetry and sweep points. The headend receiver (SCU-1800/SDA, or the RPD/RPU orchestrated by XPERTrak on DAA nodes) measures them and sends the results back to the meter.
- Each marker shows the Headend level, the Meter level and the Delta between them.
- The SCU-1800 recommended input is 0 dBmV within ±20 dBmV.
- The injection specs conflict: the EQSG lists +20 to +50 dBmV, while a template example shows 8.0 dBmV with 20 dB TPC.
- VIAVI recommends active sweep for alignment (response under 1 s) and DOCSIS checks for final validation.

No source defines a 'balanced' versus 'swept' done criterion. The company procedure has to supply it.

items.appliesTo: Quantum18 SA balancing philosophy
items.values: The guide states that auto-alignment lets the amplifier adjust itself to provide unity gain within the network RF design, without the field level measurements normally needed in RF setup. Once initial installation is complete there is no field-level adjustment of levels, downstream or upstream. The process is the same for HGD and HGBT.

items.appliesTo: Quantum18 SA reverse troubleshooting / verification
items.values: Reverse RF can be measured at the module reverse input and reverse output test points. Confirm proper reverse input from the downstream amplifier at the reverse input TP first; the amp cannot be balanced without proper reverse input. Configure per the design print and allow about 1 hour warm-up. Use the proper total tilt reference when setting receive levels. Gain check (first-pass paraphrase): measure the main reverse input TP and the reverse output TP, then subtract the reverse amplifier gain and add pad values and EQ insertion loss to confirm proper reverse gain. If the problem persists, rerun Upstream alignment in QuantumLink Local.

first_pass.summary:
Every finding below was read from primary SCTE or CableLabs pages using Firecrawl only. No third-party mirrors were used.

(1) SCTE 293-5 2024, "What is … Unity Gain?", is an SCTE Industry Reference monograph from the Network Operations Subcommittee, released 12/23/24. Its definition (4.2) says each amplifier's gain equals the loss of the cable and passives just upstream of it, so the net gain from one amplifier to the next is 0 dB.
- Forward (5.1, 5.1.1): the reference point is the amplifier output.
- Return (5.1.2): the reference point is at the same physical place, but in signal-flow terms it is each return amplifier's input. Footnote 7 places that input at the common point of the downstream output diplex filter.
- Return pads and EQs sit at the return amplifier outputs because return spans branch.
- Footnote 6: in a working network, equalizer insertion loss also counts toward unity gain.
- The full PDF downloaded from the CableLabs library with no login, and the SCTE FAQ says all SCTE standards are free to download.

(2) SCTE 293-7 2025, "What is … Long Loop Automatic Level Control?", released 2/17/25, is not a plant-alignment document. It describes DOCSIS station maintenance: the CMTS uses RNG-RSP messages to move each modem's transmit level until the received level matches the CMTS target set point (RLSP), which defaults to 0 dBmV on most CMTSs and is configurable. Its link to return alignment is indirect. Adding a pad at the CMTS input raises upstream levels in the plant, including the node input, and can cause laser clipping or push modems to their maximum transmit level. Long-loop ALC corrects the total upstream attenuation end to end; it does not set unity gain at each amplifier (this last point is my inference).

(3) The SCTE operational practice that covers return balancing is SCTE 180 2025, "Recommended Practices for Coaxial Cable Construction and Testing", released 10/20/2025 and now free.
- It separates rough balance (13.2.2), which sets near-correct RF levels with a signal level meter, from system alignment (13.3), which is frequency-response or sweep testing. This is a direct source for a "balanced" versus "swept" done check.
- The return path keeps a constant input level at the unity gain reference point (UGRP). Three balancing methods are listed. If the correct level is injected at the UGRP, the correct level arrives at the headend.
- A return sweep reference trace is stored with the source injected at the node.
- The source level equals the desired level at the UGRP plus the insertion-point loss. Pad and EQ are then adjusted until the headend response matches the reference.
- 13.7.1 explains the choice of UGRP (gain block, diplex common port or station port). Modern designs prefer the diplex common port.
- 13.7.2 gives source-level matrices (Tables 12 and 13), transcribed below.
- SCTE 180 gives no numeric headend receive target for the return sweep.

(4) ANSI/SCTE 279 2022, "1.8 GHz Broadband Radio Frequency Hardline Amplifiers for Cable Systems", is a specification, not an operational practice. It never mentions unity gain.
- It does define RF test points: -20 dB, upstream accurate to ±1 dB, with an upstream injection test point on the diplex common path.
- It defines upstream operational gain, anticipated at 30-32 dB at 684 MHz for high-gain amplifiers and 4 to 7 dB for boosters.
- It requires electronically controlled upstream attenuation and equalization (no plug-in pads or EQs), upstream RF level control over temperature, and recommends an upstream ingress switch.

items.appliesTo: Unity gain definition (forward and return)
items.values: Paraphrase: unity gain is a design and operating philosophy in which each amplifier's gain in dB equals the total loss in dB of the coax and passives immediately upstream from that amplifier, so the net gain from amplifier to amplifier is 0 dB. 'Unity' means a gain of 1, which is 0 dB. Gain is defined as GdB = Pout(dBmV) - Pin(dBmV) and loss as LdB = Pin(dBmV) - Pout(dBmV).
items.locator: Section 4.2 Definitions ('unity gain', 'gain', 'loss'), pp.6-7

items.notes: A design and operating principle, not a numeric field tolerance. The document gives no pass/fail window.

items.appliesTo: Forward (downstream) amplifiers
items.values: Section 5.1: when forward unity gain exists, the input level to a span equals the output level of the amplifier after that span. Exceptions are noted, e.g. a bridger feeding a derated line extender. Cascade example: 10 identical amps, 22 dB gain, 23 dB loss per span, first output +32 dBmV, next input +9 dBmV, second output +31 dBmV, third input +8 dBmV / output +30 dBmV; tenth amp input +1 dBmV, output +23 dBmV. Section 5.1.1 (Figure 2): 22 dB amps, output +32 dBmV. Span AB 22 dB @ 750 MHz gives a +10 dBmV input with 0 dB input atten. Span BC is 2 dB coupler + 14 dB cable @ 750 MHz = 16 dB, so a 6 dB input attenuator gives +16 dBmV input. Span BD totals 19 dB, so a 3 dB input attenuator gives +13 dBmV input. All three outputs are +32 dBmV. The forward unity gain reference point is the downstream amplifier output. The goal is identical levels at the reference points in a cascade of identical amps.
items.locator: Section 5.1 (p.8, Figure 1); Section 5.1.1 Downstream Unity Gain (pp.9-10, Figure 2)
items.firecrawlCalls: firecrawl_scrape (pdf parser) https://library.cablelabs.com/server/download/3817fdd5-7932-4add-97fd-d579326add79
items.notes: Footnote 6 (p.9): the example leaves out equalizer insertion loss for simplicity, but in an operating network equalizer insertion loss is also counted for unity gain. Relevant to a worksheet that has both a pad and an EQ field.

items.appliesTo: Return (upstream/reverse) amplifiers
items.values: Section 5.1.2: unity gain in the return cascade is essential. A return amp's gain must numerically equal the loss of the cable and passives in the span immediately upstream of it. The return reference point is at the same physical location as the forward one, but in signal-flow terms it is each amplifier's input, not its output. When return unity gain exists, the input to a given amp equals the output of the span upstream of it. Footnote 7: the upstream amplifier input means the common point of the (downstream) output diplex filter, often the same physical location as the housing's downstream output port. Figure 3 example (losses at 30 MHz, identical return amps with 15 dB gain, every reference-point input +20 dBmV): span AB 4 dB loss needs an 11 dB output attenuator at amp B (output +24 dBmV). Span BC 5 dB loss needs a 10 dB output attenuator at amp C (output +25 dBmV). Span BD 8 dB passive + 2 dB cable needs a 5 dB output attenuator at amp D (output +30 dBmV). Return amps carry their attenuators and equalizers at the outputs because a branching point (amp B fed by spans BC and BD) cannot be corrected by one input pad.
items.locator: Section 5.1.2 Upstream Unity Gain (pp.10-11, Figure 3, footnote 7); Section 5.2 Conclusion (p.11)

items.appliesTo: What long loop ALC is
items.values: 4.2: ALC is a closed-loop process that keeps configured RF levels at a circuit, device or network input or output as attenuation changes. 'Net upstream attenuation' is all gains and losses between a cable modem and the CMTS/CCAP/RPD input; example: modem +45 dBmV, CMTS input 0 dBmV, so 45 dB. Section 5: during DOCSIS station maintenance (defined in MULPI) the CMTS checks the received upstream level, timing and other parameters. If the level does not match the CMTS target set point, it sends a ranging response (RNG-RSP) telling the modem to change its transmit power. The target set point defaults to 0 dBmV in most CMTSs and is user configurable. Footnote 2: the target is the receive level set point (RLSP), formerly 'commanded nominal receive power' in DOCSIS 3.0 and earlier. Footnote 3: coax attenuation in dB changes about 1% for every 10 °F, so nightly and seasonal temperature swings drive ALC corrections. Modem transmit headroom is finite.

items.appliesTo: Upstream level behavior when attenuation changes
items.values: 5.1.1 baseline: modem DS input +3 dBmV, modem US transmit +45 dBmV, tap input +43 dBmV, node +15 dBmV, CMTS 0 dBmV. 5.1.2: a 4-way splitter adds 7 dB. Before ranging: tap +36, node +8, CMTS -7 dBmV, DS at modem -4 dBmV. After RNG-RSP the modem goes to +52 dBmV, and tap +43, node +15, CMTS 0 dBmV are restored. 5.1.3: a 3 dB pad at the CMTS upstream input briefly gives -3 dBmV. Modems on that port then rise 3 dB (+45 to +48), and tap (+46), node (+18; also upstream optical receiver output) and pad input (+3 dBmV) all rise 3 dB. Benefit: upstream CNR improves by the pad value. Risks: laser clipping if the optical link is near compression, and modems already at maximum transmit cannot follow. 5.1.4: with the modem maximum at +54 dBmV and 10 dB of extra drop loss, the modem can only rise 9 dB, so tap +42, node +17, CMTS -1 dBmV, DS -7 dBmV. The fix is to repair the drop.

items.appliesTo: Return alignment versus long loop ALC
items.values: Stated: anything that changes net upstream attenuation between modems and the CMTS makes the CMTS change modem transmit power (Section 5). Padding at the headend or hub raises upstream levels throughout the coax plant and at the node, with a laser-clipping risk (5.1.3). Not stated: SCTE 293-7 does not describe return sweep, injection levels, amplifier pads/EQs or unity gain reference points. Inference (mine): ALC compensates only the end-to-end total, so return amplifier unity gain still sets where modem transmit levels and node input levels end up. SCTE 180 13.7.1 makes the related point that modem levels in homes vary with amplifier type when the reference point is poorly chosen.

items.appliesTo: Done check: balanced versus swept
items.values: 13.2.2.1: rough balancing means setting RF levels with a signal level meter (SLM). It gets near-correct levels at the actives so tap levels are adequate for initial installation, and should be done before customers are added. 13.3: system alignment is frequency-response (amplitude versus frequency) testing, i.e. sweep. It is used at initial turn-on and as part of ongoing maintenance. 13.3.1: alignment assumes the headend and optical link are set up and starts at the node, working toward end of line. 13.4: performance verification (CCN, MER, CTB/CSO, hum) should follow rough balance and sweep.

items.appliesTo: Return path balancing concept and methods
items.values: 13.2.2.2: the return path has many inputs summing into one headend/node return input. One badly set return amp can degrade the whole return node, so the return should be balanced before it is connected to the existing system. Initial return balancing means placing the correct pad and EQ to minimize noise and ingress at the headend/node. 13.2.2.2.2: forward amps are set for constant output; return amps are set for constant input. The monitoring point for a return amp is the input of the next amp, some distance away. Three methods: (1) video monitor with a multi-carrier generator; (2) SLM with an upstream carrier generator; (3) return sweep system. When the correct level is injected at the return amp's unity gain reference point, the correct input to the headend equipment results, so the headend reading is referenced to the source injected at the amp.

items.appliesTo: Return sweep equipment setup, injection and receive points
items.values: 13.2.2.3.3.1: the legacy method was a headend spectrum analyzer viewed by a camera on an unused forward channel (needs an unused 6 MHz downstream channel), with a return signal source injecting at the amp (Figure 128). Dedicated return sweep: a headend monitor measures the field unit's return signals and sends results back on a forward telemetry carrier. The field unit has a built-in source to inject known signals at the field test point (Figure 129). Modes are return sweep and ingress monitor. Setup: program telemetry carriers and a sweep table that avoids active return signals. Store a reference trace of the headend reading with the signal injected at the node, and compare later injection points against it. The reference level is tied to the constant input level required at each return amp's unity gain reference point. Connect the forward RF to the field unit input, and the field unit source output to the return injection point. 13.2.2.3.3.2: check ingress first. Check the return pad and EQ against the design. Connect the correct-level source at the return injection point and compare headend levels. Use gain/slope controls (if present) for fine adjustment. Small pad/EQ changes are acceptable, but large departures from design should be investigated before continuing.

items.appliesTo: Return amplifier sweep alignment step
items.values: 13.3.1.2: the return measurement device is usually at the headend, with display data sent on a downstream telemetry carrier. Testing requires a known, calibrated source at the amp under test. Set the return sweep transmitter output equal to the level required at the unity gain reference point plus the loss between the insertion point and the reference point. A sweep source level matrix per amplifier type is suggested (see 13.7.2). Connect the source at the return insertion point and compare the headend response with the reference response. Adjust attenuator and EQ values until the response matches the reference. Different insertion point types may need different source levels. Finally confirm forward output levels at the output test point, close the housing and move to the next station.

items.appliesTo: Where the return unity gain reference point is
items.values: 13.7.1: the forward path needs constant amplifier output (amp output to amp output). The return path needs constant input at every amp, which is return unity gain from amp to amp. The reference point may be the return gain block (hybrid) input, the common port of the diplex filter, or the station input port. It is set during design. Historically the gain block input was used (long trunk cascades, analog return video), but the loss from station port to gain block differs by amp type: very little in a line extender, up to 8 dB extra combining loss in a four-port amp. That produced different modem levels in homes depending on amp type, which modern networks cannot tolerate. Designs now prefer unity gain at the amp port, and most modern designs use the diplex filter common port as the more exact reference point. The reference point may not be reachable from a test point, so the injected source level must exceed the desired reference-point level by a factor calculated per amp or node type (Figure 133, Generic Amplifier Diagram).

items.appliesTo: Return balancing preconditions
items.values: 13.7.3: ingress (shortwave, CB/ham, power-line and appliance noise) enters where shielding is compromised and builds up at the headend. Poor return alignment affects noise and ingress levels. Powering return amps with 0 dB return pad/EQ can make enough noise to disable the whole return, which is why return levels are set before the path is combined with the active system. If ingress disrupts sweep telemetry, isolate it by disconnecting return inputs or removing return attenuators; some amps have plug-in diplex filters and splitters. Some sweep systems broadcast ingress measurements to the field unit when a threshold is exceeded.

items.values: High-gain downstream (7.2.7): every downstream output port shall have a directional test point; the downstream input port shall have one (may be directional). All downstream test points shall be -20 dB relative to the port. Output test points should be accurate to -20 dB +/- 0.5 dB and shall be accurate to -20 dB +/- 1.0 dB. Downstream output test points shall sit on the diplex common path so they can also serve for upstream injection with two-way test gear. High-gain upstream (7.3.7): each upstream input port shall have a directional input test point. The upstream output port shall have an output test point (may be directional). Each upstream input port shall also have an upstream RF injection test point on the diplex common path, which doubles as the downstream output test point. All upstream test points shall be -20 dB relative to the reference point and accurate to -20 dB +/- 1 dB. Type, loss and accuracy shall be published; measurements per SCTE 144. Booster (10.2.7/10.3.7): -20 dB relative to the port, accurate to +/- 1.5 dB, plus an upstream injection test point on the diplex common path. first_pass.topic: Cisco 1 GHz GainMaker System Amplifier (OL-31156-01) and Line Extender (OL-31155-01): reverse (return) path balancing, reverse pads, reverse EQ and test point loss
first_pass.summary:
Both 2014 Cisco GainMaker 1 GHz guides give the same reverse-balancing method, nearly word for word. I read them through third-party mirrors (manuals.plus PDFs, plus a manualzz copy of OL-31156-01). Cisco no longer serves either OL guide: the OL-31156-01 URL and the older 4009927_D Line Extender PDF return 404, and the two Wayback attempts also returned 404. The recorded data come from the mirrors. The only primary (cisco.com-hosted) sources are the GainMaker data sheets dated 2005 (Scientific-Atlanta).

What the guides establish for a station-view return worksheet:
(1) Order of work. Balance the reverse fiber link first. Then balance each coax cascade from the node outward, starting with the amplifier closest to the node and working outward from each split. Repeat for every node port.
(2) Injection point. Inject at the port's -20 dB "Forward Output and Reverse Injection" test point. On the System Amplifier this exists for Main, Aux 1 and Aux 2. The test points sit electrically outside the diplex filter, and the signal enters the reverse path ahead of the reverse amplifier.
(3) Injection level = design reverse port input level from the design print + the total injection insertion loss of 20 dB. The worked example is 19 dBmV + 20 dB = 39 dBmV.
(4) Input pad. The reverse input pad sits after the injection point. The technician either swaps it temporarily for a 0 dB pad, so injection and headend receive levels stay the same at every amplifier and port, or expects the receive level to be lower by the pad value. Design input pads must be put back afterwards.
(5) Read point. The level is read at the RF output test point of the node's reverse optical receiver in the headend or hub, and compared with a reference amplitude and tilt. If the generator is offset from the calculated level, or the sweep runs x dB below CW, the reference moves by the same amount.
(6) Adjustments. Fix tilt with the reverse output EQ. Fix level with the reverse output pad, which moves the receive level 1:1 in the opposite direction.
(7) Done check. The station is done when the receive level and tilt match the reference. The guides never use the word "unity". The closest wording is that receive levels stay constant from amplifier to amplifier and port to port. The guides also give no separate sweep-flatness ("swept") criterion, so the app has to define "swept" itself.

Accessories: pads run 0-20.5 dB in 0.5 dB steps (GM-PAD-1G-xx=). Reverse cable EQs come in 1-12 dB, 1 dB steps, as separate 40/42, 55, 65 and 85 MHz families. Loss charts are published for the 42/40, 55 and 65 MHz EQs and the 42/40 thermal EQ; there is no 85 MHz loss chart. The part number for the 0 dB reverse EQ jumper differs between tables.

The 42/54 data sheets add -20 dB ±0.5 dB test points, 19.5 dB reverse operational gain (with 0 dB input pad, 0 dB EQ and 1 dB output pad; 0.5 dB less with the reverse switch fitted) and a 35 dBmV @42 MHz reverse reference output level. Page numbers come from each guide's table of contents and in-text cross-references, which agree. The back-of-book index in both mirrors is offset by about 3 pages.

items.values: Step 1: balance the reverse fiber link (node reverse optical transmitter to headend/hub reverse optical receiver). Step 2: balance the reverse amplifier cascades that combine at the node, starting with the amplifier closest to the node and working outward. Balance all reverse amplifiers off one node reverse input port in sequence from the node outward. Check that the reverse fiber link was balanced first. items.values: Record the design pad values for each input port before balancing. Reverse input pads are chosen during design to minimize variation in return path losses between reverse inputs; do not change them permanently without a system designer. The reverse input pad comes after the reverse injection point. Option A: temporarily replace the design input pad on the port being balanced with a 0 dB pad, which keeps injection level and headend receive level the same from amplifier to amplifier and port to port. Option B: leave the pad in and expect a receive level x dB lower than normal, where x is that port's reverse input pad value. Afterwards, put the design input pads back on any port that was temporarily fitted with 0 dB.

first_pass.topic: AOI Quantum18 return (upstream) alignment and the 204/258 return sweep context (VIAVI ONX-630 / XPERTrak)
first_pass.summary:
For the station-view worksheet, the sources support these points.

(1) AOI Quantum18 SA guide V02102025, read only through the ManualsLib mirror. Upstream alignment comes after downstream setup of the whole cascade. It must start at the last amplifier in the cascade and can run in Auto or Manual mode.
- Auto mode finishes with a Save or Revert prompt.
- Manual mode requires a VIAVI ONX-630 in DOCSIS Expert mode as the measuring tool. The app exposes only Gain and Tilt, adjusted one at a time against marker frequency levels. A check box applies a change without saving it, Save Configuration commits it, and Revert returns to the factory preset so Auto Align can override.
- After both directions are aligned, ALSC (off by default) is switched ON on each amplifier in the cascade.
- Test-point routing is chosen in the app. The HGD has three -20 dB test points outside the diplex filter.
- The guide claims auto-alignment gives unity gain within the RF design without field measurements, and that levels are not adjusted in the field after setup.
- The troubleshooting page gives a reverse gain check: output test point minus input test point, with pad values and EQ insertion loss taken into account. The page still contains a draft marker.
- The guide's text has no injection level, reference level, gain/tilt range or step size. The 'Example of US settings for 750MHz' table exists only as an image, so its values could not be read.

(2) AOI QB18 HGD data sheet (PRELIMINARY; Internet Archive capture 20241107; the live AOI URL now returns 404). Reverse figures, all specified for the 204 MHz split:
- minimum operational gain 27 dB
- internal tilt 0 dB (±0.5)
- recommended operating input 9 dBmV per 6.4 MHz channel
- noise figure <9 dB
- 10 dB of dynamic range at NPR >= 55 dB

(3) VIAVI documents.
- Return sweep principle: the headend sweep unit sends forward telemetry containing the return plan. The ONX in the field transmits return telemetry and sweep points. The headend unit (SDA/SCU-1800, or the RPD/RPU orchestrated by XPERTrak RCI on DAA nodes) measures them and sends the results back to the meter.
- The meter screen shows, per marker: the Headend (received) level, the Meter transmit level, and the Delta between them. The header shows Rev TPC, Rev Telem TX/RX/Δ and Fwd Telemetry.
- The Referenced tab shows deltas against a saved reference. The Alignment tab shows chosen carriers as received at the headend.
- The SCU-1800 recommended reverse input is 0 dBmV, with a ±20 dBmV allowable range and 20 dB minimum telemetry SNR.
- The guide's spec slide lists reverse sweep injection and reverse telemetry as +20 to +50 dBmV. Its example test-point template, however, shows Reverse Sweep Injection 8.0 dBmV with Reverse TPC 20 dB. The retrieved text does not explain how these relate, so check on a real meter.
- XPERTrak keeps the same meter and workflow on R-PHY nodes.
- VIAVI recommends active return sweep for alignment because it responds to tilt, gain or EQ changes in under 1 second, versus 2-8 minutes for DOCSIS-based alignment. It positions DOCSIS testing as a supplement for final validation.

No source defines a published 'balanced' versus 'swept' done criterion. The app has to supply that from the company procedure.

Suggested mapping (my interpretation, not stated by VIAVI): injection = ONX Meter level, level at receiver = Headend marker level, and difference from target = the Headend level compared with the company receiver target.

items.appliesTo: VIAVI XPERTrak return sweep on Remote PHY / DAA nodes
items.values: Considering R-PHY brochure: VIAVI Stealth Sweep is reproduced for DAA by using the Remote PHY Unit (RPU) as the new return sweep receiver, with XPERTrak in an orchestration role. Field instruments and reverse-sweep workflows are the same on legacy and DAA nodes. XPERTrak RCI replaces the SCU-1800 for DAA nodes, and the same ONX630 meter is used. Sweeping in an Evolving Network app note: same active reverse sweep injection from the ONX in the field; telemetry and sweep interaction come from XPERTrak orchestration; response time to amp changes (tilt, gain, EQ) is <1 second; DOCSIS-based alignment can take 2-8 minutes and level changes often take 2+ minutes; DOCSIS testing is a recommended supplement for final validation; balance and align with sweep points next to OFDM-A carriers.
